<reflection>
The second experiment with added product (P=0.1 M) resulted in decreased negative log-likelihood (NLL) values for all mechanisms, indicating improved fits with additional data. M7 remains the best-fitting model, but the NLL differences among the top mechanisms (e.g., M7, M12, M17, M16) are still small, suggesting high uncertainty. The product addition did shift relative rankings slightly, providing some discrimination, particularly for mechanisms sensitive to product presence (e.g., reversible steps or product deactivation). However, my aim to significantly reduce uncertainty over the entire set was only partially achieved, as many mechanisms remain closely ranked and plausible. Further experimentation is needed to distinguish between these candidates.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To enhance discrimination across the plausible mechanisms, I propose varying the catalyst concentration while keeping substrate constant and starting with no product. Increasing the catalyst concentration to 0.05 M will probe for non-linear effects arising from catalyst-catalyst interactions, such as dimerization (relevant for M2, M3, M13, M18, M19) or catalyst activation/deactivation pathways. Mechanisms without such interactions should exhibit reaction rates approximately proportional to catalyst concentration, while those with interactions may show deviations due to shifts in equilibria or speciation. This condition avoids extreme saturation (substrate at 1.0 M is moderate) and depletion, and it introduces a new variable (catalyst level) that impacts a wide range of mechanisms simultaneously. By comparing kinetics at different catalyst concentrations, we can gain insights into the role of catalyst speciation and interactions, helping to differentiate between simple Michaelis-Menten models, dimerization-involved mechanisms, and various deactivation schemes.
</hypothesis>
